nodes.name: Mountain beech
nodes.desc: A beech tree of the park's cooler forests; Wikipedia names beech forest as one of the main forest types around Tongariro and Ruapehu.

nodes.name: Red tussock
nodes.desc: Dominant tall tussock of the volcanic plateau, growing on pumice soils. Its flower heads host fly larvae and moth caterpillars.

nodes.name: Heather
nodes.desc: Introduced for grouse shooting, it now covers over a third of the park and has displaced native plants. Red deer eat it.

nodes.name: Broadleaf (kapuka)
nodes.desc: A native broadleaf tree whose leaves and fruit are eaten by possums, pigeons and tūī.

nodes.name: River algae (periphyton)
nodes.desc: The slimy film of algae on stream stones. It feeds the insect larvae that blue ducks scour from the riverbed.

nodes.name: Red deer
nodes.desc: Introduced browser listed among the park's pests. It eats heather and also browses other plants; carcasses feed scavengers.

nodes.name: Common brushtail possum
nodes.desc: Introduced from Australia; mostly eats leaves, flowers and fruit but also takes bird eggs and chicks. Seen as a major threat to native forests and birds.

nodes.name: European hare
nodes.desc: Introduced grazer and the most-recorded mammal near the park. Eaten by falcons, harriers and stoats.

nodes.name: North Island grasshopper
nodes.desc: A short-horned grasshopper restricted to alpine and sub-alpine habitats of the North Island, including the central volcanic region.

nodes.name: Kererū (NZ pigeon)
nodes.desc: Mainly eats fruit, plus leaves, flowers and buds. Possums and rats compete for fruit and take eggs; stoats and cats kill adults and young.

nodes.name: Tūī
nodes.desc: A common native honeyeater of the park's forests, feeding on nectar and fruit.

nodes.name: Caddisfly larvae
nodes.desc: Cased caddisfly larvae are named by Wikipedia as a main food of blue ducks in fast, clean mountain streams.

nodes.name: Whio (blue duck)
nodes.desc: Endangered duck of fast, clean mountain rivers that eats mainly midge and caddisfly larvae. Stoats destroy nests and kill nesting females.

nodes.name: Tomtit (miromiro)
nodes.desc: A small insect-eating forest bird that hunts beetles, caterpillars, spiders and other invertebrates.

nodes.name: Swamp harrier (kāhu)
nodes.desc: Open-country hawk recorded near the park that hunts and also scavenges carrion; GloBI records hares, rabbits and possums as prey.

nodes.name: Stoat
nodes.desc: Introduced predator and a major threat to blue ducks; it kills nesting birds and takes hares, possums and even falcons in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Kārearea (NZ falcon)
nodes.desc: Bush falcons hunt forest edges in North Island forests. They catch mostly birds in flight, plus some hares and rabbits.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Drives growth from the forest to the alpine zone, where altitude sets the plant belts.

nodes.name: Rain & snow
nodes.desc: Rain and snow on the volcanic peaks feed the forests, tussock lands and cold fast rivers.

nodes.name: Volcanic soils
nodes.desc: Pumice and ash soils are nutrient-poor, but red tussock tolerates them across the volcanic plateau.

nodes.name: Mountain streams
nodes.desc: Cold, clean, fast-flowing rivers are the habitat blue ducks need.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi and soil invertebrates recycle dead leaves and carcasses into the soil.
